questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Identify the confound hidden in an engineering correlation
questions.stem: A design review notes that plants with the newest sensors also report the fewest unplanned stops, and proposes the sensors as the cause.

options.text: The maintenance upgrade bundled with new sensors may have cut the stops on its own
Better sensors reveal stops that were happening all along but going unrecorded before
options.misconception: treats a recording change as a change in the process

options.text: Stop counts fell because crews began recording near misses to meet the quarterly target
options.misconception: assumes reporting behaviour drives the physical process

options.text: Modernization removes further gains unless the plant modernizes again in the next cycle
options.misconception: assumes modernization leaves no room for further gains

questions.explanation: The brief pairs sensor age with fewer stops without showing the sensors drove the change. A bundled maintenance upgrade could explain both, and the other options mistake a recording effect or a ceiling for a mechanism.
questions.hint: Ask what else changed on the same date as the sensors.

The barrier must be dropped because the housing already passed without it
options.misconception: denies a necessary condition that was actually present

questions.explanation: A required component can be necessary without being sufficient, since other properties also decide the rating. Only option C states both halves correctly, while B treats necessity as guarantee and D denies a condition the test always included.

questions.learningObjective: Separate the event that set a process moving from the process itself
questions.stem: A refinery's yield chart shows a sharp step in year four and a steady climb through year nine; the brief calls year four the cause of the climb.

options.text: The steady climb shows the step had no effect on the process at all
options.misconception: reads no trend as no effect

options.text: Year four shifted the process and later improvements came from within it

options.misconception: makes one event explain every later change

options.text: The step is a plotting error because real yields never change suddenly
options.misconception: dismisses a sharp change as a graph artifact

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Timing as a test of a causal claim
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the sequence of events can test a proposed cause
questions.stem: Explain to a review board how the order of events in a retrofit programme can test a claim that the new controller raised throughput.

answer.exemplar: A causal claim predicts an order: the controller change should precede the throughput rise by at least the commissioning lag, and the rise should not appear before installation. If throughput jumped three months before the controller arrived, or stayed flat for months after it, the sequence contradicts the claim. Sequencing evidence is necessary but not sufficient, so it narrows the list of candidates rather than settling the question on its own.

questions.explanation: Timing is a cheap test because causes precede effects. A rise before the cause, or no rise long after it, weakens the claim without excluding every alternative.
questions.hint: Ask what should have happened first, and when.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how method can change while function remains continuous
questions.stem: Explain to a planning committee how an organisation can change sharply in method while remaining continuous in function.

answer.exemplar: Continuity of function means the same task keeps being performed and the same dependencies keep working, even when the method is replaced. Naming the unchanged functional commitments makes the change assessable, because each redesign can be checked against them one by one.

questions.explanation: Continuity and change apply to different layers of the same organisation. Holding the function steady lets the method change be judged against commitments rather than against a fantasy of starting over.
questions.hint: Separate what must survive from what may be replaced.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how to separate a cause from enabling conditions
questions.stem: Explain to a new engineer how a cause differs from the conditions that make a cause effective.

answer.exemplar: A cause is the element whose removal would remove the effect, while conditions are the background that lets the cause act. In the pump example, the impeller is the cause of the flow loss and the inlet strainer condition is only a condition on it. Holding the conditions fixed lets the engineer test the cause alone, and it also explains why the same cause can matter more or less in different installations of the same machine.

questions.explanation: Separating cause from condition tells you which change to test and which context to hold steady. Without that separation, improvements get credited to whatever was nearest in the record.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain the difference between a required and a guaranteeing condition
questions.stem: Explain to an auditor how to tell a necessary condition for a result apart from a sufficient one, using the load cell calibration example.

answer.exemplar: A necessary condition must be present for the result to occur, so its absence rules the explanation out, while a sufficient condition guarantees the result whenever it is present. Quarterly calibration of the load cells may be required for the scale to read within legal tolerance, but calibration alone cannot guarantee that, because drift, load and geometry also bear on it. An auditor who keeps the two apart can demand the missing half of the reasoning and can spot a claim of guarantee disguised as a claim of requirement.

questions.explanation: Confusing the two produces both false guarantees and false dismissals. Keeping them apart lets a reviewer see exactly which half of the reasoning has been supplied and which has been assumed.
questions.hint: Ask whether the condition guarantees the result or requires it.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how background weakness shapes what an event does
questions.stem: Explain to a local history group how a long structural weakness can shape what a single dramatic event does to a town.

answer.exemplar: A flood or a fire works on whatever conditions it meets, so two towns hit by the same storm can end differently because of silted canals, narrow streets or fragile roofs. The structural weakness is present before the event and quietly raises the damage, and the event then makes that weakness visible. Naming the background first also explains why rebuilding to the same pattern produced similar losses the next time, and it points to the change that would actually reduce risk.

questions.explanation: Structural conditions decide how much damage an event can do, so they belong in the account before the event is described. An explanation that lists only the drama leaves the repeated losses unexplained.

questions.learningObjective: Read a flat long-run series that contains large short-run swings

stimulus.body: A municipal water table record covering ninety years shows almost no net change in the average level. Individual drought years show falls of four to six metres and wet years show rises of similar size. The engineer signing off the record notes that the site has never been abandoned.

questions.stem: Given this record, which description of the aquifer fits the evidence best?

options.text: Flat readings mean the aquifer never responded to the climate at all
options.misconception: treats no net change as no response whatsoever

options.text: A ninety-year record with no net change cannot be used for any purpose
options.misconception: dismisses a whole record because its endpoint matches

options.text: Short-run variation means the long-run figure is the least meaningful number
options.misconception: dismisses the long-run signal because short-run noise exists

options.text: The aquifer holds a stable long-run level while varying sharply in the short run

questions.explanation: A flat long-run line can sit on top of large swings, and the two facts are compatible. The long span shows the system is resilient in aggregate, not that it ignores the weather it lives in.
questions.hint: Look at the swings inside the flat long run.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Timing as a test of a causal claim
questions.learningObjective: Explain how record order tests a claim about fuel use
questions.stem: Explain to a commissioning team how the order of records can test a claim that a heat recovery unit cut boiler fuel use.

answer.exemplar: A causal claim predicts an order, so the test is whether the effect appears only after the cause and at the size the mechanism predicts. Boiler logs show fuel use falling sharply three months before the unit was commissioned, which rules the unit out as the explanation for the earliest fall and points to another driver such as a fuel price change. Timing tests are necessary but not sufficient, so a favourable order still leaves the need to consider coincident changes.

questions.explanation: Timing tests are cheap and decisive when they fail: an effect that precedes its cause rules that cause out. A favourable order narrows the field without excluding coincident drivers.
questions.hint: Ask what should have happened first, and when.

questions.learningObjective: Explain a major technical change that leaves service continuity intact
questions.stem: Explain to a transport authority how a signalling replacement can be a major change that leaves the network's continuity intact.

answer.exemplar: The network's continuity rests in services continuing to run and connections remaining usable, not in the particular equipment that carries them. Replacing signalling changes the method by which trains are spaced and protected, and that is a substantial technical change, yet the same routes keep working for the same passengers. The test the authority should apply is to name the commitments that must not break, then check the new signalling against them one by one rather than approving or rejecting it wholesale.

questions.explanation: Change at the level of method and continuity at the level of function can both be true. Naming the commitments that must survive turns a general approval into a testable decision.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how to distinguish a failure's cause from its enabling conditions
questions.stem: Explain to a reliability engineer how to tell a cause of a failure from the conditions that made the failure possible.

answer.exemplar: A cause is the change whose removal would prevent the failure, while a condition is the standing state that made the change consequential. If a pipe failed after a pressure spike on a line whose fittings were already corroded, the spike is the proximate cause and the corrosion is a condition that raised the odds. The distinction matters for action: correcting the condition lowers the odds across many failure routes, while correcting the cause only addresses the route that was actually taken.

questions.explanation: Blurring cause and condition sends engineers to fix only the trigger and leave the permissive background in place. Naming both levels tells the team where each remedy actually acts.
questions.hint: Ask which change, if undone, prevents the failure.

questions.learningObjective: Compare a targeted group's position against a stated aim
questions.stem: A school's aim is to raise attendance in the lowest income band; that band's attendance is 78 percent against 94 percent for the school average.

options.text: The aim has been met, because the programme has been running for two years
options.misconception: treats time spent as evidence of result

options.text: Attendance cannot be compared between groups, so the aim cannot be assessed
options.misconception: rules out comparison rather than making it carefully

options.text: The lowest position proves the programme has already done all it can
options.misconception: treats a poor ranking as proof of maximal effort

options.text: The aim and the group's position diverge, and the programme needs review

questions.explanation: An aim is measured against the condition it targets, and here the targeted group is still well below the comparison. That divergence calls for review of the programme rather than a reinterpretation of the figures.
questions.hint: Ask how the target group compares with the others.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how drainage condition shapes the damage from a given rainfall
questions.stem: Explain to a council why a flood's damage depends on the condition of the drainage system as well as on the rainfall.

answer.exemplar: The same volume of rain does the same amount of work on the street, and the drainage system decides how much of it the street can absorb. Silted drains turn a heavy hour into a flood, while a maintained network keeps the same rain as a nuisance. That is why a rebuild that restores the old drain pattern tends to reproduce the old losses, and why the structural condition deserves more attention in the plan than the rainfall figure usually receives. Events are shocks; the drainage condition is what sets the price of being shocked.

questions.explanation: Structural conditions decide how much damage an event can do, so they belong in the account before the event is described. An explanation that lists only the drama leaves the repeated losses unexplained.
questions.hint: Ask what state the drains were in when the rain came.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Read stability at one level of a long record against turnover below it

stimulus.body: A town's tax roll for 120 years shows the same five family names in the highest band in every decade, while the names beneath them turn over almost completely between 1460 and 1520 and again between 1580 and 1640. The clerk notes that the town was not destroyed or depopulated in either period of turnover.

questions.stem: Given this roll, which description fits the record best?

options.text: The changing names show the town's leadership was never stable at all
options.misconception: reads turnover at one level as instability everywhere

options.text: Continuity sits at the top of the roll while turnover runs beneath it
The stable top five show the town was frozen and nothing could change within it
options.misconception: infers total rigidity from continuity at the top

options.text: A 120-year tax roll cannot support any claim about continuity at all
options.misconception: dismisses a long record instead of reading it

questions.explanation: Long records often show stability at one level and constant replacement at another, and that combination is what continuity with change looks like. The alternatives read either change or stability at the wrong level.
questions.hint: Look at which level of the roll stays stable.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Frame a substantial project against the commitments that must survive
questions.stem: A hospital replaces paper ward rounds with a shared digital handover board; which sentence holds both the change and the continuity together?

options.text: The handover method changes and the ward round continues to happen daily
The hospital has changed, so the continuity of care must now be questioned
options.misconception: lets the change swallow the continuity

options.text: The hospital remains continuous, so the handover change needs no assessment
options.misconception: lets the continuity swallow the change

options.text: Continuity rests on commitments that survive, not on methods staying the same
options.misconception: defines continuity as a rule about unchanged methods

questions.explanation: Change at the level of method and continuity at the level of commitments can coexist, and naming the commitments is what makes the judgement possible. The alternatives either deny the change or deny that continuity is testable.
questions.hint: Ask which commitments the project must preserve.
